Primary goals: define success criteria (quality thresholds and latency SLOs), gather workload sizing (qps, avg tokens), establish benchmark plan and timeline for hosted vs Dedicated infra, and shortlist 3-4 open models with quantization/latency recommendations.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Head of ML - Skyline), Daniel Ruiz (CTO), Asha Menon (Data Eng Lead), Marco Silva (PM)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, can you hear me OK?
[00:06] Priya Patel: yep loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:10] Maya Chen: awesome. quick agenda — scope the POC success criteria, get concrete workload numbers, talk model shortlist (open models), and then outline benchmarks and timeline. sound good?
[00:20] Daniel Ruiz: yes that's perfect. we want to make sure this won't just be a toy test — production-ish workloads and multilingual evaluation are important.
[00:28] Liam O'Rourke: cool, i'll jump in on the benchmark part later, but first, priya — can you walk us through the expected traffic and what "success" looks like?
[00:36] Priya Patel: sure. our main product ingests geo-event reports in 4 languages — english, spanish, french, japanese — clients ask for summaries and entity extraction plus a short risk-score. average payload is ~420 tokens, sometimes up to 1,200 for long reports. baseline qps today is small — roughly 4 rps average, spike to 30 rps during batch windows. concurrency target for us is sustained 20 concurrent requests with 50 reqs/sec peak.
[01:04] Marco Silva: timeliness matters — we need 95th p99 latency under 900ms for summary endpoints, the extraction can be looser — p95 under 1.5s acceptable.
[01:14] Maya Chen: helpful — so success criteria: quality thresholds for summaries (ROUGE-ish or human eval pass rate), entity extraction precision/recall min, and latency SLOs as stated. is there a baseline model you're comparing to?
[01:24] Priya Patel: we ran a quick comparison vs an off-the-shelf instruct-tuned model (third-party API) — it's okay for english but drops on spanish/japanese. we'd like to see parity across languages or at least a defined delta. quality baseline: human eval >= 85% pass for summaries on EN/ES/FR and >= 80% on JP.
[01:40] Liam O'Rourke: got it. on the model front, since you asked for open models, my recommendation is to shortlist 3-4 candidates spanning sizes and instruction tuning. initial candidates we typically bring: Llama 3 70B (if available/compatible), Mistral-Instruct family (7B/8B variants), Falcon-40B-Instruct, and MPT-30B or Mosaic models. each has tradeoffs on multilingual support and cost.
[02:04] Priya Patel: can you say more about the multilingual tradeoffs — we can't afford to have japanese be terrible.
[02:08] Liam O'Rourke: sure — generally larger models (>=30B) with instruction tuning handle japanese better out-of-the-box than smaller 7B models, but quantization and GPU memory can limit latency. for example, Llama-family and Falcon often show strong multilingual performance; Mistral 8B is excellent in many benchmarks for european languages but historically weaker for east asian scripts, though recent instruction-tuned variants improved.
[02:32] Maya Chen: also worth noting our Redwood Optimize tooling can recommend quantization profiles — int8/llm.int8 vs int4 — and suggest dedicated GPUs for low p99 latency. that will affect cost and throughput.
[02:42] Daniel Ruiz: curious — what's the rough cost delta for running Llama 3 70B vs Mistral 8B on Redwood Dedicated? just ballpark.
[02:49] Maya Chen: ballpark, if you're running 20 concurrent requests, 70B models typically need multi-GPU or GPU with larger memory and will be ~3-4x the token cost versus a 7-8B model in int8. with int4 and kernel optimizations you can shrink that gap but quality tradeoffs sometimes appear. i'll include estimates in the model matrix.
[03:07] Asha Menon: from infra side — we need VPC peering, SSO (SAML), and KMS integration for keys. also log retention controls, and audit logs for compliance.
[03:18] Maya Chen: that's standard for Private deployments; for the hosted POC we can do VPC peering and customer-managed KMS with Dedicated or Private. i'll surface our SOC2/ISO docs.
[03:26] Priya Patel: about benchmarks — we want to test end-to-end latency including our network and the model inference, and also run a quality sweep across the same prompts in four languages.
[03:35] Liam O'Rourke: recommended plan: 1) dry run on hosted Redwood with smaller batch to sanity-check prompts, 2) perf benchmark runs for each model candidate capturing latency p50/p95/p99, throughput, and cost per 1k tokens, 3) quality runs using your labeled set + blind human eval on a sample of 200 prompts per language. we'll instrument token-level timing so we can separate network vs inference.
[04:00] Marco Silva: timeline? we want results before end of next month.
[04:03] Maya Chen: doable — propose this timeline: sample dataset by 2027-05-06, Redwood shares shortlist + perf/cost matrix 2027-05-04, run benchmarks 2027-05-10 to 2027-05-12 (72-hour runs per model), quality eval completed by 2027-05-18, wrap and review 2027-05-20.
[04:20] Daniel Ruiz: that fits our timeline. what about fallback strategies if a model fails quality? can we cascade to a larger model only for failed/lang edge cases?
[04:29] Liam O'Rourke: yes — Redwood supports smart routing/fallbacks; you can route by policy to a higher-tier model for languages or prompt types that need it. also prefix caching and KV cache can speed repeated contexts. keep in mind routing increases cost complexity.
[04:43] Priya Patel: for domain adaptation — will fine-tuning be part of POC or do we do prompt engineering + retrieval?
[04:49] Maya Chen: to keep the POC quick, we recommend retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) + prompt engineering first; if quality doesn't meet criteria we can add a small fine-tune or LoRA step in a second phase. we can include a LoRA experiment in the benchmark plan as an optional run.
[05:02] Asha Menon: likely retrieval first — less ops overhead. also curious about tokenization/language handling — will all models support utf-8 languages equally?
[05:09] Liam O'Rourke: tokenizers differ — some models have better tokenization for CJK scripts. that's one reason larger multilingual models tend to do better on Japanese, since their vocab/tokenizer handles it more effectively. we'll capture tokenization overhead in the benchmark.
[05:25] Priya Patel: what would you shortlist initially — please be concrete so we can agree.
[05:28] Maya Chen: initial shortlist (we'll send full matrix):
- Falcon-40B-Instruct (strong mid-size multilingual, good for EN/ES/FR)
- Llama-3-70B-Instruct (best-in-class for multilingual — higher cost)
- Mistral-Instruct-8x or Mistral-7B-Instruct (good perf/cost, check JP behavior)
- MPT-30B-Instruct or MosaicML-30B (domain-friendly, strong long-context handling)
[05:59] Daniel Ruiz: can you include a lightweight 7B baseline too so we see delta? maybe Mistral-7B.
[06:04] Liam O'Rourke: yep we'll include a 7B baseline to show improvement curve. for each model we'll profile: latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput qps, cost per 10k tokens, tokenization overhead, and human-eval quality per language.
[06:18] Marco Silva: any considerations on batching? we don't want batching to add latency for single requests.
[06:24] Liam O'Rourke: Redwood supports adaptive batching; for low-latency single requests we can set max-batch-size=1 and use latency-first routing. for cost-heavy periods we can allow larger batches with slightly higher p95. these are tunable in the POC.
[06:38] Priya Patel: security — we need to know where logs live, retention, and whether any customer data persists on model hosts.
[06:45] Maya Chen: by default Redwood does not persist customer prompts beyond configured retention; for Dedicated and Private you control disk and retention policies. i'll attach the security appendix and KMS flow.
[06:55] Daniel Ruiz: good. one subtlety — what about quantization quality regressions? some models show hallucination increases with aggressive quantization.
[07:03] Liam O'Rourke: true — int4 can sometimes change generation patterns. we'll run both int8 and int4 for sensitive examples, and include automated checks for hallucination rates (entity hallucination). that will be part of the benchmark matrix.
[07:16] Maya Chen: ok wrapping up — recap next steps?
[07:20] Priya Patel: we'll share sample data, and agree to the shortlist/matrix from Redwood.
[07:24] Maya Chen: i'll send the shortlist + cost/perf estimates by 2027-05-04, liam will publish the benchmark plan, and we'll target runs starting 2027-05-10.
[07:33] Marco Silva: sounds good, thanks all.
[07:36] Daniel Ruiz: thanks Maya, talk soon.
[07:39] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. end.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap and mis-typed product names may appear; this export preserves natural speech patterns and minor ASR errors.
